title: Robert Schumann Announces Brahms
text:
On September 30, 1853, a shy, fair haired young pianist of twenty knocked at the door of Robert and Clara Schumann in Dusseldorf. Johannes Brahms came from a poor family in Hamburg, had earned money playing piano from an early age, and was almost unknown. He carried a letter of introduction from the violinist Joseph Joachim.

Brahms sat down and began to play one of his own piano sonatas. Robert Schumann soon stopped him and called Clara in to hear it from the start. That evening Robert noted in his diary a visit from Brahms, "a genius." For the next weeks Brahms was almost part of the household.

Schumann had not written for his old music journal in years. On October 28, 1853, he published an article titled "Neue Bahnen" (New Paths), announcing Brahms as the young man destined to give the highest expression to the age, one who had sprung forth fully armed. It made Brahms famous overnight, and placed a heavy expectation on him.

A few months later Robert suffered a breakdown and was confined to an asylum. Brahms stayed close, helping Clara and the children. His friendship with Clara lasted until her death in 1896.
lesson: If you see real talent in someone unknown, say so publicly and back it with your name. A single act of recognition can change the course of a life.
people: Robert Schumann, Johannes Brahms, Clara Schumann, Joseph Joachim
source: Robert Schumann, "Neue Bahnen," Neue Zeitschrift fur Musik, October 28, 1853; Robert Schumann's household diaries
